item.title: What to know about the Army’s lead detonation in Iowa
item.description:
After months of planning, days of warnings, and the fear of a plume of lead dust, the destruction of nearly 5 tons of unstable explosives in southeastern Iowa was over in seconds. For all the concern about what might happen when the U.S. Army blew up 68 drums of lead azide on Wednesday, the detonation itself proved remarkably uneventful. Two booms sounded across a clear, cold winter morning just after 9 a.m., each creating a wispy white plume that quickly dissipated. State and federal officials said the operation appeared to have gone as planned, and more than an hour later, the Environmental Protection Agency’s real-time air monitors had detected no airborne lead . Officials had warned that the detonation could send lead-laden dust over homes and farmland for miles around.
